# Research question and design

**Can chemical measurements predict a red wine's sensory quality, and does a
flexible local model outperform a regularized linear model?** I compare two
methods permitted by the assignment: **linear regression with ridge
regularization** and **k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) regression**. An ordinary least
squares model and a training-mean predictor provide reference points.

I chose the red-wine portion of the [UCI Wine Quality dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/186/wine+quality).
It has a manageable sample size, numerical predictors on very different scales,
and correlated measurements. These properties make scaling, shrinkage, and
model complexity meaningful. Qulity is an ordered score. Regression preserves
that ordering and penalizes large errors more heavily, while assuming equal
spacing between adjacent scores. The goal is prediction, not a causal claim
about changing a wine's chemistry.

The original contribution is a from-scratch implementation of both models,
repeated cross-validation with scaling learned inside each fold, and a split
that prevents identical chemical prfiles from appearing on both sides of a
training/validation boundary. The final model is chosen using training-set
cross-validation before the held-out test set is scored.

# Data, source, and quality checks

The data creators are Paulo Cortez, A. Cerdeira, F. Almeida, T. Matos, and J.
Reis (2009). The red-wine file contains **1,599 observations, 11 chemical
predictors, and one sensory quality score**. It concerns Portuguese red Vinho
Verde wines. The documented score scale is 0–10; the observed range is checked
below. The source documentation describes the score as the median of at least
three expert evaluations. UCI distributes the dataset under CC BY 4.0.

The original semicolon-delimited dataset, `winequality-red.csv`, is included
with this project. No internet connection is needed to rerun the analysis.

The next chunk reads the original file, verifies the schema, and constructs a
profile identifier from the predictors alone. It does not silently remove
outliers or repeated rows. Repeated profiles may represent duplicate entries
or separate samples; without sample identifiers, their origin is uncertain.
Keeping their rows together is a conservative way to prevent exact-profile
leakage while preserving the dataset's original observation weights.

```{r import-and-check}
# read.csv2 uses semicolons but expects comma decimals, so specify read.csv.
wine <- read.csv("winequality-red.csv", sep = ";", check.names = TRUE)
predictors <- setdiff(names(wine), "quality")
stopifnot(nrow(wine) == 1599L, length(predictors) == 11L,
          all(vapply(wine, is.numeric, logical(1))), !anyNA(wine),
          all(is.finite(as.matrix(wine))), all(wine$quality %in% 0:10))

# A profile ignores quality so even matching inputs with differing labels
# must stay together. Each unique profile receives an integer group ID.
profile_key <- do.call(paste, c(wine[predictors], sep = "|"))
group_id <- match(profile_key, unique(profile_key))
audit <- data.frame(
  Check = c("Rows", "Predictors", "Missing cells", "Exact repeated rows",
            "Repeated predictor profiles beyond the first", "Unique profiles",
            "Minimum quality", "Maximum quality"),
  Value = c(nrow(wine), length(predictors), sum(is.na(wine)),
            sum(duplicated(wine)), sum(duplicated(profile_key)),
            length(unique(group_id)), min(wine$quality), max(wine$quality)))
knitr::kable(audit, caption = "Data audit (all rows; no fitted preprocessing).")
```

There are `r sum(duplicated(wine))` exact repeated rows and
`r length(unique(group_id))` unique chemical profiles. A naive row-wise split
could place identical inputs in training and testing, especially benefiting
nearest neighbors. All splits in this analysis operate on the profile groups.
All numerical values are finte and none are missing, so imputation is
unnecessary. Unusual measurements are retained because no documented error
rule justifies removing them.

| Variable | Role / meaning |
|:--|:--|
| fixed.acidity, volatile.acidity, citric.acid | Acidity measurements |
| residual.sugar | Residual sugar measurement |
| chlorides | Chloride measurement |
| free.sulfur.dioxide, total.sulfur.dioxide | Free and total sulfur dioxide |
| density | Wine density |
| pH | Acidity on the pH scale |
| sulphates | Sulphate measurement |
| alcohol | Alcohol measurement |
| quality | Target: sensory score, documented 0–10 scale |

## Hold-out split before exploratory analysis

I randomly reserve 20% of the unique profiles for testing and use the remaining
80% for training and tuning. The percentages of rows can differ slightly from
80/20 because groups have different sizes. Test outcomes do not influence
feature exploration, scaling, model selection, or tuning. A random split
estimates performance on similar unseen profiles; it does not evaluate future
vintages or a different geographic region.

```{r grouped-split}
# Fixing the seed makes the same group allocation reproducible.
set.seed(402)
all_groups <- sort(unique(group_id))
train_groups <- sample(all_groups, floor(0.80 * length(all_groups)))
in_train <- group_id %in% train_groups
train <- wine[in_train, , drop = FALSE]
test <- wine[!in_train, , drop = FALSE]
g_train <- group_id[in_train]
g_test <- group_id[!in_train]
stopifnot(length(intersect(g_train, g_test)) == 0L)

# Preserve row identifiers and allocation so the split can be audited.
split_file <- data.frame(row_id = seq_len(nrow(wine)), group_id = group_id,
                         split = ifelse(in_train, "train", "test"))
write.csv(split_file, "results/split_assignments.csv", row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Split = c("Training", "Test"), Rows = c(nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  Profiles = c(length(unique(g_train)), length(unique(g_test)))),
  caption = "The test set remains outside all tuning.")
```

## Training-set exploration

The distribution plot shows whether the response is balanced across scores.
The correlation plot uses predictors only and helps motivate ridge regression:
correlated columns can make unregularized coefficients sensitive to the sample.
Neither plot establishes causation.

```{r training-exploration, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Training-set quality distribution and predictor correlations."}
# Use training rows for all exploratory plots. Correlations do not rescale data.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.3, 4.4, 2.5, 1))
barplot(table(factor(train$quality, levels = 3:8)), col = blue, border = NA,
        xlab = "Quality score", ylab = "Training observations",
        main = "Most scores are in the middle")
corr <- cor(train[predictors])
short_names <- c("Fixed acid", "Volatile acid", "Citric acid", "Sugar",
                 "Chlorides", "Free SO2", "Total SO2", "Density", "pH",
                 "Sulphates", "Alcohol")
par(mar = c(7.5, 7.5, 2.5, 1))
image(seq_along(predictors), seq_along(predictors), corr,
      zlim = c(-1, 1), col = colorRampPalette(c(orange, "white", blue))(101),
      axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Predictor correlations")
mtext("Orange = -1; white = 0; blue = +1", side = 3, line = .2, cex = .65)
axis(1, at = seq_along(predictors), labels = short_names, las = 2, cex.axis = .68)
axis(2, at = seq_along(predictors), labels = short_names, las = 2, cex.axis = .68)
box()
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Report the strongest pair by absolute correlation, excluding the diagonal.
pair_index <- which(upper.tri(corr), arr.ind = TRUE)
pair_index <- pair_index[which.max(abs(corr[pair_index])), ]
top_pair <- predictors[pair_index]
top_correlation <- corr[pair_index[1], pair_index[2]]
training_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(train), Minimum = sapply(train, min),
  Mean = sapply(train, mean), SD = sapply(train, sd), Maximum = sapply(train, max))
knitr::kable(training_summary, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Training-set descriptive statistics in original units.")
```

Scores 5 and 6 account for
`r fmt(100 * mean(train$quality %in% c(5, 6)), 1)`% of training observations.
Consequently, a model can obtain a reasonable overall error while performing
poorly on rare low or high scores. The strongest absolute predictor correlation
is between `r top_pair[1]` and `r top_pair[2]`
(`r fmt(top_correlation)`). The standard deviations also vary considerably
across columns, so unscaled Euclidean distances would favor large-scale variables.

# Methods and their implementation

## Training-only standardization

Each predictor is transformed to `(x - training mean) / training SD`. Ridge
needs comparable predictor scales because its penalty acts on coefficients;
kNN needs them because distance determines the neighbors. In cross-validation,
the mean and standard deviation come only from the fold's analysis rows, then
the same transformation is applied to validation rows. For the final fit, they
come from the full training set. The response is not standardized.

```{r scaling-functions}
# Store the fitted transformation separately from applying it to new rows.
fit_scaler <- function(x) {
  center <- colMeans(x)
  spread <- apply(x, 2, sd)
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(spread)), all(spread > 0))
  list(center = center, spread = spread)
}
apply_scaler <- function(x, scaler) {
  sweep(sweep(as.matrix(x), 2, scaler$center, "-"),
        2, scaler$spread, "/")
}
```

## Ridge regression: a regularized linear model

Ridge minimizes **mean squared training error + lambda × sum of squared
slopes**. The intercept is unpenalized. With centered responses and standardized
predictors, its slopes are obtained by solving
`(Z'Z/n + lambda I) beta = Z'(y - mean(y))/n`.
Dividing the loss by `n` makes the penalty convention explicit. A package with a
different loss convention may report a different numerical lambda for the same
fit. At lambda = 0, this is ordinary least squares. Larger lambda shrinks the
slopes toward zero, usually increasing bias and reducing variance. Ridge keeps
all predictors; it does not perform subset selction.

The function below fits an entire lambda grid. `crossprod` computes matrix
products efficiently, and `solve(A, b)` solves a linear system without forming
an explicit inverse. Centering the response lets the intercept be recovered as
the training mean when predictors are standardized with training statistics.

```{r ridge-function}
ridge_path <- function(z, y, newz, lambdas) {
  n <- nrow(z)
  p <- ncol(z)
  y_mean <- mean(y)
  gram <- crossprod(z) / n
  rhs <- crossprod(z, y - y_mean) / n

  # Each column contains one fitted model's standardized slopes.
  beta <- vapply(lambdas, function(lambda) {
    as.numeric(solve(gram + diag(lambda, p), rhs))
  }, numeric(p))
  rownames(beta) <- colnames(z)
  list(pred = sweep(newz %*% beta, 2, rep(y_mean, length(lambdas)), "+"),
       beta = beta, intercept = y_mean)
}
```

## k-nearest-neighbor regression: a local mean

For each new wine, kNN finds the `k` closest training rows using Euclidean
distance on standardized predictors, then averages their quality scores. No
linear relationship is assumed. Small `k` permits a highly variable local fit;
large `k` produces a smoother fit with more bias. With `k` equal to the training
sample size, every prediction is the training mean. In 11 dimensions, distance
can be less informative than in one or two dimensions, which is a limitation.

Teh identity `||a-b||² = ||a||² + ||b||² - 2 a'b` computes all squared distances.
Their order is the same as that of Euclidean distances, so square roots are
unnecessary. `pmax` guards against tiny negative values from rounding. Ties are
resolved by training-row order, which is deterministic. Cumulative sums obtain
predictions for many values of `k` after sorting each query's distances once.

```{r knn-function}
knn_path <- function(z, y, newz, ks) {
  stopifnot(all(ks >= 1L), max(ks) <= nrow(z))
  distance2 <- pmax(outer(rowSums(newz^2), rowSums(z^2), "+") -
                      2 * tcrossprod(newz, z), 0)
  predictions <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(newz)), function(i) {
    nearest <- order(distance2[i, ], seq_along(y))
    cumulative_y <- cumsum(y[nearest])
    cumulative_y[ks] / ks
  }, numeric(length(ks)))
  # Preserve query-by-k shape even when only one k or one query is supplied.
  t(matrix(predictions, nrow = length(ks), ncol = nrow(newz)))
}
```

# Repeated cross-validation and model selection

I use **five repetitions of five-fold grouped cross-validation** within the
training set. Each profile is held out once per repetition. Both methods use
the same folds for a fair comparison. Fold allocation balances the number of
profiles approximately; it does not guarantee equal row counts or score counts.

The tuning grids include 0 (OLS) plus 55 positive ridge penalties from 0.0001
to 1,000, and 15 neighbor counts from 1 to 501. The selected setting minimizes
pooled validation RMSE, giving each held-out row equal weight. RMSE is the
square root of average squared error, in quality-score points. Unlike training
error, cross-validation error evaluates predictions for rows excluded from the
fit. Its minimum is still subject to selection optmism, which is why a
separate test set is retained.

```{r grouped-cross-validation}
# Set grids before looking at any test performance.
lambdas <- c(0, 10^seq(-4, 3, length.out = 55))
ks <- c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21, 31, 45, 65, 95, 151, 251, 501)
folds <- 5L
repeats <- 5L
train_x <- as.matrix(train[predictors])
train_y <- train$quality
groups <- sort(unique(g_train))
ridge_sse <- numeric(length(lambdas))
knn_sse <- numeric(length(ks))
ridge_fold_rmse <- matrix(NA_real_, repeats * folds, length(lambdas))
knn_fold_rmse <- matrix(NA_real_, repeats * folds, length(ks))
fold_record <- list()
total_validation_rows <- 0L
cv_row <- 0L
set.seed(403)

for (rep_id in seq_len(repeats)) {
  # Randomize group-to-fold assignments independently for each repetition.
  group_fold <- sample(rep(seq_len(folds), length.out = length(groups)))
  row_fold <- group_fold[match(g_train, groups)]
  fold_record[[rep_id]] <- data.frame(
    row_id = which(in_train), group_id = g_train,
    repetition = rep_id, fold = row_fold)

  for (fold_id in seq_len(folds)) {
    validation <- row_fold == fold_id
    analysis <- !validation
    stopifnot(!any(g_train[validation] %in% g_train[analysis]))

    # Crucially, validation rows do not contribute to scaling statistics.
    scaler <- fit_scaler(train_x[analysis, , drop = FALSE])
    za <- apply_scaler(train_x[analysis, , drop = FALSE], scaler)
    zv <- apply_scaler(train_x[validation, , drop = FALSE], scaler)
    ya <- train_y[analysis]
    yv <- train_y[validation]
    ridge_predictions <- ridge_path(za, ya, zv, lambdas)$pred
    knn_predictions <- knn_path(za, ya, zv, ks)

    # Accumulate squared error, then pool over rows rather than folds.
    ridge_error <- sweep(ridge_predictions, 1, yv, "-")^2
    knn_error <- sweep(knn_predictions, 1, yv, "-")^2
    ridge_sse <- ridge_sse + colSums(ridge_error)
    knn_sse <- knn_sse + colSums(knn_error)
    cv_row <- cv_row + 1L
    ridge_fold_rmse[cv_row, ] <- sqrt(colMeans(ridge_error))
    knn_fold_rmse[cv_row, ] <- sqrt(colMeans(knn_error))
    total_validation_rows <- total_validation_rows + length(yv)
  }
}

ridge_cv <- sqrt(ridge_sse / total_validation_rows)
knn_cv <- sqrt(knn_sse / total_validation_rows)
ridge_best <- which.min(ridge_cv[-1]) + 1L  # tune positive ridge penalties
knn_best <- which.min(knn_cv)
best_lambda <- lambdas[ridge_best]
best_k <- ks[knn_best]
selected_family <- if (ridge_cv[ridge_best] <= knn_cv[knn_best]) "Ridge" else "kNN"
selection <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Ridge", "kNN"),
  Parameter = c(paste("lambda =", signif(best_lambda, 5)), paste("k =", best_k)),
  CV_RMSE = c(ridge_cv[ridge_best], knn_cv[knn_best]))
knitr::kable(selection, digits = 4, caption = "Tuning results; test outcomes unused.")
write.csv(do.call(rbind, fold_record), "results/cv_fold_assignments.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(selection, "results/model_selection.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

The selected ridge penalty is **`r signif(best_lambda, 5)`**, with CV RMSE
**`r fmt(ridge_cv[ridge_best], 4)`**. The selected neighbor count is
**`r best_k`**, with CV RMSE **`r fmt(knn_cv[knn_best], 4)`**.
**`r selected_family` is the chosen model family**, based only on these
cross-validation results. OLS has CV RMSE `r fmt(ridge_cv[1], 4)`.
The ridge candidate grid is restricted to positive penalties; OLS is reported
separately as its zero-penalty reference. No tuning choice is changed in
response to the later test scores.

## Complexity curves and the bias–variance tradeoff

The following curves compare in-sample training RMSE with grouped validation
RMSE. Both the final training fit and the validation folds are computed with
their appropriate scaling. kNN's training predictions include the query row
itself and possibly identical rows; especially at `k = 1`, this is an
optimistic in-sample fit, not an estimate of predictive accuracy. The grouped
validation curve is the relevant tuning criterion.

```{r complexity-curves, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Training and grouped cross-validation error as model complexity changes. Vertical lines mark the selected settings."}
# Final training fits let us visualize the gap between fit and generalization.
final_scaler <- fit_scaler(train_x)
z_train <- apply_scaler(train_x, final_scaler)
ridge_training <- ridge_path(z_train, train_y, z_train, lambdas)
knn_training <- knn_path(z_train, train_y, z_train, ks)
ridge_train_rmse <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(ridge_training$pred, 1, train_y, "-")^2))
knn_train_rmse <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(knn_training, 1, train_y, "-")^2))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
positive <- lambdas > 0
matplot(lambdas[positive], cbind(ridge_train_rmse[positive], ridge_cv[positive]),
        type = "l", log = "x", lty = c(2, 1), col = c(orange, blue), lwd = 2,
        xlab = "Ridge penalty lambda (log scale)", ylab = "RMSE",
        main = "Ridge: shrinkage")
abline(v = best_lambda, lty = 3, col = green)
legend("topleft", c("Training", "Grouped CV"), col = c(orange, blue),
       lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .8)
matplot(ks, cbind(knn_train_rmse, knn_cv), type = "l", log = "x",
        lty = c(2, 1), col = c(orange, blue), lwd = 2,
        xlab = "Neighbors k (log scale)", ylab = "RMSE",
        main = "kNN: neighborhood size")
abline(v = best_k, lty = 3, col = green)
legend("bottomright", c("Training (includes self)", "Grouped CV"),
       col = c(orange, blue), lty = c(2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = .75)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Store the full grids and fold variation for independent inspection.
write.csv(data.frame(lambda = lambdas, training_RMSE = ridge_train_rmse,
                     CV_RMSE = ridge_cv,
                     SD_fold_RMSE = apply(ridge_fold_rmse, 2, sd)),
          "results/ridge_tuning.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(k = ks, training_RMSE = knn_train_rmse,
                     CV_RMSE = knn_cv,
                     SD_fold_RMSE = apply(knn_fold_rmse, 2, sd)),
          "results/knn_tuning.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

At `k = 1`, training RMSE is `r fmt(knn_train_rmse[1])`, but validation RMSE
is `r fmt(knn_cv[1])`. At the selected `k = r best_k`, validation RMSE is
`r fmt(knn_cv[knn_best])`; by `k = r max(ks)` it is
`r fmt(tail(knn_cv, 1))`. Very small neighborhoods can fit individual observations
closely but transfer poorly to unseen profiles. Very large neighborhoods
average chemically different wines and can miss useful local patterns. The
intermediate tuning result illustrates the practical bias–variance tradeoff.

For ridge, validation RMSE changes from `r fmt(ridge_cv[1])` at zero penalty
to `r fmt(ridge_cv[ridge_best])` at the selected penalty and
`r fmt(tail(ridge_cv, 1))` at the largest penalty. Strong shrinkage pushes the
model toward a constant and causes underfitting. The CV improvement over OLS
is only `r fmt(ridge_cv[1] - ridge_cv[ridge_best], 4)` points of RMSE, so
regularization adds little predictive value beyond this linear fit.
Ridge is not guaranteed to improve every dataset. Thse curves demonstrate
training/generalization behavior, not a numerical decomposition of bias and
variance. Repeated CV folds overlap, so fold variation is descriptive rather
than a set of independent observations or a confidence interval.

# Held-out test performance

Only now are the fitted models applied to the test set. Each tuned method uses
all training observations and the selected tuning parameter. The mean baseline
predicts the training-set average for every test wine. OLS uses exactly the
same predictors as ridge. Predictions are kept continuous and are neither
rounded nor clipped.

I report RMSE (primary), mean absolute error (MAE), test R-squared, and the
fraction of predictions within one score point of the observed outcome.
Test R-squared is `1 - SSE / sum((y_test - mean(y_test))^2)`; it can be negative.
The within-one measure is a supplementary tolerance measure, not exact
classification accuracy. Because a constant prediction can be within one
point for many middle-score wines, it must be interpreted alongside RMSE.

```{r test-evaluation}
# Test features are scaled using the full training statistics, never their own.
z_test <- apply_scaler(as.matrix(test[predictors]), final_scaler)
ridge_test <- ridge_path(z_train, train_y, z_test, lambdas)$pred
knn_test <- knn_path(z_train, train_y, z_test, ks[knn_best])[, 1]
test_prediction <- list(
  "Mean baseline" = rep(mean(train_y), nrow(test)),
  "OLS" = ridge_test[, 1], "Ridge" = ridge_test[, ridge_best], "kNN" = knn_test)
metrics <- function(actual, predicted) {
  error <- actual - predicted
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean(error^2)), MAE = mean(abs(error)),
    R_squared = 1 - sum(error^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2),
    Within_one = mean(abs(error) <= 1))
}
test_results <- data.frame(Model = names(test_prediction),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(test_prediction, function(p) metrics(test$quality, p))),
  row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(test_results, digits = 4,
             caption = "Held-out test results; lower RMSE/MAE is better.")
write.csv(test_results, "results/test_metrics.csv", row.names = FALSE)
test_export <- data.frame(row_id = which(!in_train), group_id = g_test,
                          actual = test$quality, check.names = FALSE)
for (nm in names(test_prediction)) test_export[[nm]] <- test_prediction[[nm]]
write.csv(test_export, "results/test_predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# All narrative numbers below are computed from the actual model outputs.
selected_prediction <- test_prediction[[selected_family]]
selected_result <- test_results[test_results$Model == selected_family, ]
baseline_result <- test_results[test_results$Model == "Mean baseline", ]
rmse_reduction <- 100 * (1 - selected_result$RMSE / baseline_result$RMSE)
```

The model chosen by CV, **`r selected_family`**, obtains test RMSE
**`r fmt(selected_result$RMSE)` quality points**, MAE
**`r fmt(selected_result$MAE)`**, and test R-squared
**`r fmt(selected_result$R_squared)`**. Its RMSE is
**`r fmt(rmse_reduction, 1)`% lower than the training-mean baseline**.
The mean absolute error means predictions miss by about
`r fmt(selected_result$MAE, 2)` score points on average; it does not mean that
every prediction is within that distance. The within-one fraction is
`r fmt(100 * selected_result$Within_one, 1)`%, compared with
`r fmt(100 * baseline_result$Within_one, 1)`% for the baseline.

kNN's test RMSE is `r fmt(test_results$RMSE[test_results$Model == "kNN"], 4)`,
slightly below ridge's `r fmt(selected_result$RMSE, 4)`. Teh test ordering
therefore differs from CV; switching models after seeing this result would
turn the test set into another selection set. Ridge also improves on OLS by
only `r fmt(test_results$RMSE[test_results$Model == "OLS"] - selected_result$RMSE, 4)`
points of test RMSE. The main gain here comes from using the measured
predictors rather than from ridge regularization itself.

```{r test-comparison, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Test RMSE for the baseline, OLS, and the two tuned models."}
par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
bar_centers <- barplot(test_results$RMSE, names.arg = test_results$Model,
                      col = c("#A8ADB3", "#7E9EAA", blue, orange), border = NA,
                      ylim = c(0, max(test_results$RMSE) * 1.15),
                      ylab = "Test RMSE (quality points)", main = "Held-out prediction error")
text(bar_centers, test_results$RMSE,
     labels = fmt(test_results$RMSE), pos = 3, cex = .9)
```

# Interpretation and diagnostic plots

## Ridge coefficients and shrinkage

Ridge coefficients below represent a one-training-SD increase in a predictor,
holding other measured predictors fixed. They are conditional associations,
not experimental effects. Correlated predictors share information, so their
individual coefficient signs and ranks should not be treated as a unique
ranking of chemical importance. Ridge shrinks the coefficient vector overall;
individual slopes need not shrink monotonically when predictors are correlated.

```{r coefficient-plot, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="OLS and ridge slopes on the same standardized predictor scale."}
ridge_beta <- ridge_training$beta[, ridge_best]
ols_beta <- ridge_training$beta[, 1]
coefficient_table <- data.frame(Variable = predictors, OLS = ols_beta,
                               Ridge = ridge_beta, row.names = NULL)
ordered <- order(abs(ridge_beta))
par(mar = c(4.5, 9.5, 2.5, 1))
plot(ridge_beta[ordered], seq_along(ordered), pch = 19, col = blue,
     xlim = range(c(ols_beta, ridge_beta, 0)) * 1.15,
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Quality points per training SD",
     main = "Conditional slopes: OLS versus ridge")
axis(2, at = seq_along(ordered), labels = short_names[ordered], las = 1, cex.axis = .8)
points(ols_beta[ordered], seq_along(ordered), pch = 1, col = orange, cex = 1.1)
abline(v = 0, lty = 3, col = "gray55")
legend("bottomright", c("Ridge", "OLS"), col = c(blue, orange), pch = c(19, 1), bty = "n")
write.csv(coefficient_table, "results/standardized_coefficients.csv", row.names = FALSE)
strongest_positive <- names(which.max(ridge_beta))
strongest_negative <- names(which.min(ridge_beta))
```

The largest positive standardized ridge slope is for **`r strongest_positive`**
(`r fmt(max(ridge_beta))` score points per training SD), and the most negative is
for **`r strongest_negative`** (`r fmt(min(ridge_beta))`). This describes
conditional relationships in the fitted sample. It cannot show that
deliberately increasing or decreasing a chemical would improve sensory quality.

## Prediction quality across the score range

The observed-versus-predicted plot should lie near the diagonal for a strong
model. Vertical separation from the diagonal is error. A horizontal concentration
of predictions near the middle would indicate regression toward typical scores.
The residual plot uses `observed - predicted`, so positive residuals mean
underprediction and negative residuals mean overprediction. Horizontal jitter
only separates overlapping integer scores visually; no metric uses jittered data.

```{r test-diagnostics, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Held-out diagnostics for the family selected by cross-validation."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2.5, 1))
set.seed(405)
plot(jitter(test$quality, amount = .07), selected_prediction,
     pch = 19, col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = .35),
     xlim = c(2.8, 8.2), ylim = range(c(3, 8, selected_prediction)),
     xlab = "Observed quality (jittered)", ylab = "Predicted quality",
     main = paste(selected_family, ": observed vs predicted"))
abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = orange)
residual <- test$quality - selected_prediction
plot(selected_prediction, residual, pch = 19,
     col = adjustcolor(blue, alpha.f = .35),
     xlab = "Predicted quality", ylab = "Observed - predicted",
     main = "Residuals on unseen profiles")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = orange)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Score-specific errors expose performance hidden by an overall average.
by_score <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(test$quality)), function(score) {
  rows <- test$quality == score
  data.frame(Observed_score = score, N = sum(rows),
             Mean_prediction = mean(selected_prediction[rows]),
             Mean_residual = mean(residual[rows]),
             MAE = mean(abs(residual[rows])))
}))
knitr::kable(by_score, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = paste("Test diagnostics by observed score for", selected_family))
write.csv(by_score, "results/errors_by_score.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

At the lowest observed test score (`r min(test$quality)`), the average prediction
is `r fmt(by_score$Mean_prediction[1], 2)`; at the highest score
(`r max(test$quality)`), it is `r fmt(tail(by_score$Mean_prediction, 1), 2)`.
These values show how well the extremes are recovered rather than relying only
on the many scores in the middle. Rare-score rows in the table have small
sample sizes, so their error estimates are especially unstable. Residual
patterns can suggest missed structure, but this held-out inspection is
diagnostic only: the present models are not retuned using it.
The parallel diagonal bands in the residual plot arise mechanically because
the observed score is an integer: for each fixed score, residual equals that
score minus the prediction. The bands alone do not demonstrate nonlinearity.

# Conclusions and limitations

The analysis answers the research question with a reproducible comparison:
**`r selected_family` was selected by repeated grouped CV and achieved test
RMSE `r fmt(selected_result$RMSE)`**, versus
`r fmt(baseline_result$RMSE)` for a training-mean prediction. This is a
`r fmt(rmse_reduction, 1)`% reduction in RMSE. Chemical measurements contain
predictive information, but the remaining errors and score-specific diagnostics
show that they do not fully determine expert sensory scores.

The complexity curves explain why good training fit is insufficient. A tiny
kNN neighborhood can follow individual training observations; an excessively
large neighborhood loses local information. Ridge instead trades coefficient
flexibility for stability, and heavy shrinkage ultimately underfits. The
appropriate balance was estimated from held-out training folds, not from the
test set. 

Several limitations remain:

- **Ordered response:** treating scores as numeric assumes equal score
  intervals. An ordinal model would be a reasonable future comparison.
- **Population and dependence:** these results apply to similar red Vinho
  Verde profiles. Winery, batch, vintage, and sample IDs are unavailable.
  Grouping exact profiles cannot account for all possible dependence, nor
  guarantee performance on future vintages, white wines, or other regions.
- **Imbalanced scores:** common middle scores dominate average errors;
  rare extreme-score performance is less reliable. No artificial balancing
  was used because this analysis targets the original score distribution.
- **Model assumptions:** ridge uses additive linear relationships; kNN uses
  equal-weight Euclidean distances and is sensitive to irrelevant dimensions.
  Neither model explicitly handles all possible interactions or measurement noise.
- **Evaluation uncertainty:** there is one outer train/test split. Repeated
  inner CV reduces sensitivity to fold assignment, but does not remove tuning
  optimism. 
- **Association:** coefficients are not causal effects. Missing information
  about grapes, brands, and other context may explain part of the residual error.

A useful extension would repeat the outer grouped split or use nested grouped
cross-validation to assess the stability of the selected family. Batch or
vintage identifiers would enable a more realistic external validation. Those
extensions should use fresh validation data rather than repeatedly optimizing
against the test set reported here.

# Reproduction and references

The analysis uses base R for modeling, with knitr and rmarkdown for reporting.
To reproduce the report, place wine_quality_report.Rmd and winequality-red.csv
in teh same folder, open the R Markdown file in RStudio, and click Knit.
The code regenerates the plots and supporting result files automatically.

**Data and provenance**

1. Cortez, P., Cerdeira, A., Almeida, F., Matos, T., & Reis, J. (2009).
   *Wine Quality* [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository.
   [Dataset DOI: 10.24432/C56S3T](https://doi.org/10.24432/C56S3T).
2. Cortez, P., Cerdeira, A., Almeida, F., Matos, T., & Reis, J. (2009).
   Modeling wine preferences by data mining from physicochemical properties.
   *Decision Support Systems, 47*(4), 547–553.
   [Article DOI: 10.1016/j.dss.2009.05.016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2009.05.016).
3. Original files downloaded on November 1, 2026 from
   [UCI's Wine Quality download](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/186/wine+quality.zip).
   Only winequality-red.csv is modeled. The original dataset is included unchanged.
   [CC BY 4.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

**Method reference**

4. James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2021).
   *An Introduction to Statistical Learning, with Applications in R* (2nd ed.).
   Chapters 2, 5, and 6 discuss flexibility, cross-validation, and regularization.
   [Official book site](https://www.statlearning.com/).
